result: The authors used laser-stimulated fluorescence (LSF) imaging to examine over 100 Solnhofen pterosaur fossils, selecting four exceptional specimens for detailed imaging. LSF revealed soft tissue preservation in tail vanes, with vane areas fluorescing pink and white, and revealed hidden anatomical details not visible under white light in some specimens.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the methods as 'compelling' and noted they 'give new detail on tail morphology.' The editor stated the 'new methods are compelling,' indicating acceptance of the LSF methodology and its ability to reveal soft tissue structures.

result: The authors provide detailed morphometric descriptions of tail vanes from multiple specimens, documenting their diamond-shaped morphology, dimensions (lengths of 700-750 mm, widths of 30-55 mm), angles, and the number of caudal vertebrae encompassed (15-17). The vanes make up approximately 21-22% of total tail length.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these morphological descriptions and measurements. The editor noted the methods 'give new detail on tail morphology,' implicitly accepting these detailed morphometric data as valid contributions.

result: LSF imaging revealed internal structural details of the tail vanes, including 10-17 relatively straight, hollow, rod-like vertical structures (0.6-1 mm thick, spaced 3-8 mm apart) projecting near-perpendicularly to the tail skeleton. In one specimen (NHMUK PV OR 37003), a second layer of thinner subhorizontal fibres was observed, forming a cross-linked lattice. The data contradict previous interpretations associating these structures with neural spines and haemal arches.
evaluation: Reviewers stated the paper 'presents new evidence for soft-tissue strengthening of vanes using exciting new methods,' directly affirming these structural observations. The editor noted the findings have 'potential to resolve how pterosaurs were able to control and maintain tail stiffness,' indicating acceptance of the lattice structure findings.

result: The authors provide background on material stiffness principles, defining the modulus of elasticity (E) and explaining how stress and strain relate to deformation. They describe how pterosaur wings experienced auto-cambering under aerodynamic load and how stiffening mechanisms (muscles, keratinization, actinofibrils) limited excessive stretching by having high tensile E values.
evaluation: Reviewers noted 'there is now some discussion of bias in the sample selection method as well as some theory to show how the lattice could have functioned,' indicating acceptance of the theoretical biomechanical framework. These background principles were not challenged.

result: The authors propose that the tail vane would have experienced asymmetric airflow during flight, causing aeroelastic flutter that produces high drag unless tensioned. They argue the cross-linked lattice of vertical structures and subhorizontal fibres functioned as tensile-loaded structures (analogous to actinofibrils in wings) that resisted stretching in multiple directions, with loads taken up at the tail tip. The undulated vane edge morphology is interpreted as preserving the unloaded slack condition.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated 'there is now some discussion...as well as some theory to show how the lattice could have functioned, other than a narrative description,' indicating acceptance of the biomechanical functional interpretation. The editor noted the work has 'potential to resolve how pterosaurs were able to control and maintain tail stiffness to furnish flight control.'

result: The authors found no evidence of active muscle-based tensioning in the tail vane and propose the soft tissue lattice was the primary stiffening adaptation. While acknowledging they cannot determine the precise material composition or calculate absolute deflections, they infer the lattice would have substantially increased the elastic modulus of the vane in tension, possibly by an order of magnitude.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these interpretations or the acknowledged limitations. The statement that the lattice 'could have stiffened the vane by a large margin - probably an order of magnitude' is presented as reasonable inference given the observational data, and reviewers accepted the functional interpretation.

result: The authors conclude that the tail vane maintained effective stiffness dynamically through internal tension of the cross-linked lattice, minimizing flutter and drag. This structural integrity would have permitted the vane to function as an effective display structure without excessive aerodynamic costs and allowed the tail to be used for mass-shifting-based aerodynamic control without adverse fluttering effects.
evaluation: The editor stated the work represents 'a valuable contribution to ongoing research efforts to decipher the flight abilities of pterosaurs' with 'potential to resolve how pterosaurs were able to control and maintain tail stiffness to furnish flight control.' This indicates acceptance of the main functional conclusions.

result: The authors note that tail vane shape varies through ontogeny and between species, underscoring its evolutionary importance. They propose that in pterodactyloid pterosaurs, which evolved shorter body plans with anterior centers of mass and cranial crests, the control and display functions of the tail were absorbed by wings and head.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these evolutionary interpretations. The editor's statement that the work contributes to understanding 'flight abilities of pterosaurs in the fields of paleontology, comparative biomechanics, and bioinspired design' implicitly accepts these evolutionary context claims.

result: The authors propose the tail vane developed as a single contiguous structure (not scales or feather-like integuments) consisting of bilateral fleshy folds comparable to cetacean flukes, with connective tissue beneath an epidermal layer. They suggest ontogenetic shape changes parallel cetacean fluke development and speculate both may have evolved through shared developmental mechanisms involving co-option of appendage outgrowth signaling pathways.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these developmental and comparative anatomical interpretations. The speculative nature of the shared developmental mechanism claim is appropriately qualified with 'it is possible' and 'perhaps,' and reviewers raised no concerns about these inferences.
